pl-l3d25c5-d1e115.summary: States the thesis that faith, hope, charity, and works are in some respect equal in the present life.
claims: Faith, hope, charity, and works are equal in some respect in this life.

pl-l3d25c5-d1e118.summary: Gregory: in this life faith, hope, charity, and work are equal in us, since we love as much as we believe, hope as much as we love, and act as much as we believe, love, and hope. Yet charity is greater, because when we reach the sight of God faith and hope pass but charity remains, and because it is the mother of all virtues; it is placed after faith and hope not because it arises from them but because it will remain, increased, after them. The equality is to be understood according to the intensity of interior acts.
claims: The degrees of believing, hoping, loving, and acting are proportionate in this life.
Charity is greater because it alone remains in the vision of God.
Charity does not arise from faith and hope.
The equality concerns the intensity of interior acts.

pl-l3d25c5-d1e133.summary: Raises an objection to the claim that charity is not from faith and hope: Paul says charity is the end of the commandment, from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, which Augustine reads as pure intellect, good hope, and unfeigned faith. Thus faith and hope seem to precede charity.
claims: 1 Timothy 1:5 seems to make charity proceed from faith and hope.
Augustine reads the pure heart as intellect and good conscience as hope.

pl-l3d25c5-d1e158.summary: Resolves the objection: faith and hope do not precede charity, the mother of all goods, in causality or time; charity is said to proceed from them because it cannot exist in anyone without them, whereas they can exist without charity, though not as pious faith or hope.
claims: Faith and hope do not causally or temporally precede charity.
Charity cannot exist without faith and hope.
Faith and hope can exist without charity, but are not then pious.
Charity 'proceeds' from them only in the sense of presupposing them.

pl-l3d25c5.summary: Holds with Gregory that faith, hope, charity, and works are in a sense equal in this life, since we believe, love, hope, and act in equal measure, the equality being understood by the intensity of interior acts. Charity is nonetheless greater because it remains when faith and hope pass away, and it is the mother of virtues. Against the objection from 1 Timothy 1:5 (charity 'from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith'), Lombard explains that charity is said to proceed from faith and hope not by causal or temporal priority but because charity cannot exist without them, while they can exist (though not as pious) without charity.
claims: Faith, hope, charity, and works are equal in this life in the intensity of interior acts.
Charity is greater because it remains in glory and is the mother of virtues.
Charity does not arise from faith and hope.
Charity is said to proceed from faith and hope because it never exists without them.
Faith and hope can exist without charity, but not as pious virtues.
